title: New Hubble image of spiral galaxy ESO 137-001
caption: The spiral galaxy ESO 137-001, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: ESO 137-001 · constellation Triangulum Australe · about 220 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESAAcknowledgements: Ming Sun (UAH), and Serge Meunier

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Intense blue streaks stream outward from the spiral galaxy ESO 137-001 in this Hubble image, shining brightly in ultraviolet light. The galaxy is framed against a bright background as it travels through the heart of the galaxy cluster Abell 3627.

Those streaks are hot, wispy streams of gas that the galaxy's surroundings are ripping away from it. The space inside a cluster is not empty but filled with thin, hot gas. As the galaxy moves through it, that gas pushes back like a strong wind.

The process is called ram pressure stripping, a drag force felt by any object moving through a fluid, similar to what you feel pushing a hand through water. For a galaxy, the effect can be severe. Gas is the raw material for new stars, so losing it this way can eventually starve the galaxy of the fuel it needs to keep forming them.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.89 x 1.97 arcminutes) and distance (220 million light years), the frame spans roughly 185,000 × 126,000 light-years. Its light set out about 220 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, with ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The streaks shine in ultraviolet light, which the eye cannot see, so they would be invisible without Hubble.
